title: How One Prescription Created a Global Addiction Crisis
fullText: In 1955, a chemist at a Swiss drug company almost threw out a compound he had given up on two years earlier. He had shelved it because it refused to react the way his research called for. And during a routine lab cleanup, he decided to test it anyway, almost as an afterthought, mostly to clear space on his bench. By the early 1970s, that same abandoned compound was the single most prescribed drug in the United States, taken by tens of millions of people every year, filling medicine cabinets in suburban homes from coast to coast. This is the story of how one almost discarded molecule became a household name, sedated a generation, hid a decadesl long dependency crisis in plain sight, and quietly wrote the marketing playbook a future opioid company would use to devastating effect. But this story does not begin in a laboratory. It begins with a much older problem. For as long as medicine has existed, physicians have [music] searched for a chemical off switch for anxiety, for the racing mind, for the sleepless night. In the 1850s, doctors began prescribing potassium broomemide, a salt originally studied as a treatment for epilepsy as a catchall seditive for nerves, insomnia, and what the era's physicians vaguely diagnosed as hysteria. Broomemides were cheap, widely available, and handed out with almost no oversight. They were so heavily used, and so badly misused that doctors coined a new diagnosis just to describe the damage. Broomemide poisoning marked by confusion, skin rashes, tremors, and in severe cases, full psychosis brought on by nothing more than long-term doctor approved use. Victorian era nerve specialists built entire practices around prescribing broomemide salts to fashionable overworked patients, packaging ordinary exhaustion and marital unhappiness as a medical condition requiring their particular tonic. The drug became so associated with dullness and repetition that the word broomemide entered everyday English as slang for a stale overused saying, a linguistic fossil of the first modern seditive crisis. Alcohol tinctures and opium laced tonics filled the same role for anyone who could not get a bromide prescription. sold openly inarmacies with labels that promised calm nerves and said almost nothing about what was actually inside the bottle. Patent medicine companies of the era competed to package these ingredients [music] into ever more elaborate tonics. Each one claiming to be gentler and more modern than the last while quietly containing the same handful of sedating compounds. Then in 1864, [music] German chemist Adolf von synthesized a new compound in his laboratory and called it barbaturic acid, reportedly naming it after a woman named Barbara. For decades, the compound sat as a chemical curiosity. It took until 1903 for two other chemists, Emil Fischer and Joseph von Maring [music] to turn that base chemistry into the first commercial barbiterate. A seditive sold under the name Verinol. It was marketed as a genuine medical breakthrough. A scientific answer for a modern nervous age defined by new industrial pressures and city living. It worked and it worked well. And once the door was open, it did not close again. Over the following decades, chemists raced to synthesize variations on the formula, eventually producing more than 2500 distinct barbiterate compounds. They became fixtures of early 20th century medicine. prescribed for insomnia, for the vague catch-all diagnosis of nerves, and [music] for the shattered psychological state of soldiers returning from two world wars with what doctors of the time called shell shock and battle fatigue. Military physicians in both conflicts administered barbiterate sedation to soldiers experiencing acute psychological breakdowns on the front lines. Sometimes using it to induce a kind of deep extended sleep intended to reset a shattered nervous system before sending the soldier back into combat days later. The practice was crude by modern standards, but it reflected a genuine widespread demand for any tool that could quiet an overwhelmed mind quickly. A demand that would only grow once soldiers returned home to civilian life, carrying the same unresolved trauma with them. But barbbitures were never just medicine. They became genuinely glamorous. By the 1930s and4s, pills with brand names like Senel and Nebutil were tucked into the makeup bags of Hollywood's biggest stars. Studio doctors handed them out after grueling amphetaminefueled shooting days so exhausted actors could actually sleep before the next call time, then handed out something to wake them back up again the next morning. A chemical loop that quietly became routine on studio lots across the country. A sleeping pill became a quiet status symbol. The sophisticated fix for the anxious, overworked, and famous, a small, glamorous secret passed from one starlet to the next, whispered about in gossip columns without ever being named outright. Ordinary households picked up the same habit without any of the glamour attached. By the 1950s, barbiterates were sitting in medicine cabinets across the country, prescribed by family doctors for everything from a restless night to a difficult menopause to a child who would not settle down. Pharmaceutical companies ran full page magazine advertisements aimed directly at general practitioners, [music] presenting the pills as an uncomplicated, almost routine tool for a modern doctor's black bag. No different from aspirin or cough syrup. Pharmacists filled prescriptions for these pills so routinely [music] that entire families sometimes shared a single household bottle without anyone involved thinking of it as anything more unusual than sharing a bottle of aspirin and casual undocumented pattern of use that made the [music] drugs true reach across the population almost impossible to measure at the time. But there was a serious problem hiding underneath the glamour. Barbiterates have an extremely narrow safety margin. The gap between a dose that calms a person down and a dose that stops their breathing entirely is dangerously small. [music] And mixing that dose with a single drink can erase the line completely. Overdose deaths climbed for decades. So did suicides since a bottle of sleeping pills sitting on a nightstand was for many a genuinely lethal weapon within reach. Coroners of the era grew accustomed to a grim recurring pattern. A patient prescribed a routine sleeping pill, a bad night, a few too many tablets taken in confusion or despair, and a death that on paper looked identical, whether it had been intentional or accidental. In 1962, Marilyn Monroe died of a barbiterate overdose. and her death put the drug's deadly reputation on the front page [music] of nearly every newspaper in the country, turning what had been a quiet ongoing public health problem into a topic of open national conversation for the first time. Medicine now had an urgent, very public problem to solve. Find something that could calm the mind the way barbbiterates did without constantly risking the patients life in the process. Enter Leo Sternbach, a chemist working at Hoffman Lar Ro's research laboratories in New Jersey. In the early 1950s, Sternbach had been experimenting with an obscure class of dye compounds that stubbornly refused to behave the way his research demanded. And after repeated failures, he set the project aside entirely, moving on to other work and largely forgetting about it. In 1955, while cleaning out his lab to make room for new work, his assistant found a small stockpile of the abandoned compounds still sitting on a shelf. And rather than simply discarding them, Sternbach decided to send a few off for routine pharmacological testing, almost out of idle curiosity, expecting nothing more than a negative result that would let him finally close the book on the project. What he found instead stunned him. The compound calmed anxiety, relaxed muscle tension, and suppressed seizures. And it did all of this without anything close to the barbiterates razor thin deadly safety margin. It was, by any reasonable measure, an accident twice over, an accidental discovery inside a project that had already been declared a failure. Rosh patented the compound as Claudia epipoxide and launched it commercially in 1960 under the brand name Librium. 3 years later in 1963 [music] a chemically refined follow-up compound launched under an even more famous name Valium. Ro marketed both drugs aggressively and directly to physicians as the modern safe answer to a problem that had haunted medicine for half a century. Chemically, both drugs belong to a family built around a shared ring structure, which is where the entire drug class eventually took its name, benzoazipene. Sternbach did not stop there. Over the following years, his laboratory and rival companies churned out an entire generation of chemical cousins built on the same core structure. Drugs like clonazopam sold as clonopin and laorazzipam sold asan. Each one aimed at a slightly different symptom. Insomnia, seizures, panic, but all of them sharing the same basic mechanism and ultimately the same risks [music] of dependence that would not become widely acknowledged for decades. What followed was not a plantation and it was not a mine. [music] It was a marketing machine and it was aimed with striking precision. Rosh's sales representatives flooded doctor's offices with free samples, sponsored dinners, [music] and glossy print advertising campaigns built specifically around women as the target customer. Magazine and television ads showed a harried, overwhelmed housewife handed a small pill so she could simply get through her day, smiling again, managing the kids, the house, and her husband without complaint. One recurring advertising trope showed a woman surrounded by the chaos of daily domestic life, framed almost like a small crisis, resolved instantly and completely by a single tablet with no mention of how long she might need to keep taking it. Trade publications aimed at doctors [music] ran full page spreads describing the ideal candidate for the drug in strikingly broad terms. Essentially any woman experiencing stress from her circumstances, which in practice meant nearly anyone at all. Ordinary stress, loneliness, grief, and frustration were quietly reframed as a diagnosible, medically treatable condition. Something a woman should not have to simply endure. Prescribing became so casual, so routine that some doctors wrote fully refillable prescriptions on a patient's very first visit with no follow-up appointment required, no real conversation about how long the pill should be taken or what stopping them might feel like. The scale of what happened next is almost impossible to overstate. By 1978, Valium became the first drug in pharmaceutical history to sell over a billion tablets in the United States in a single year. For five consecutive years running through the early to mid 1970s, it held the title of the single most prescribed medication in the entire country, outs selling every antibiotic, every painkiller, and every heart medication on the market combined. To put that [music] in perspective, roughly one in every 10 American adults filled a Valium prescription at some point during the drug's peak years. An adoption rate more typical of a household staple like aspirin than a controlled psychiatric medication. A compound Sternbach had nearly thrown in the trash on an ordinary afternoon had become within two decades the bestselling drug on Earth. And the human cost hiding behind that extraordinary success is [music] staggering. Dependence on these drugs can take hold in a matter of weeks, not years, often before a patient or their doctor even notices a problem developing. Overdose deaths involving bzzoazipines in the United States climbed from close to a thousand a year in the late 1990s to more than 12,000 a year by the early 2020s. a more than 10-fold increase in [music] roughly two decades. Roughly 40% of people who take these drugs for more than 6 months go on to experience moderate to severe withdrawal symptoms once they try to stop. About 1 in four long-term users develops a withdrawal syndrome that drags on for well over a year. sometimes marked by seizures, panic, hallucinations, and a form of delirium that can turn fatal if it is not carefully managed by a physician. Doctors monitoring long-term users have also found that patients who continue taking these drugs are significantly more likely to attempt overdose than those who successfully taper off. A pattern serious enough that researchers have described the drugs themselves as capable of amplifying the very despair they were originally prescribed to relieve. For patients caught in this cycle, stopping without careful medical supervision is its own kind of danger [music] since abrupt discontinuation after long-term use can trigger the same seizures and delirium seen in the worst barbiterate withdrawals [music] decades earlier. the exact risk this entire drug class was invented to eliminate. Ro did not just profit from anxiety. Ro helped manufacture the very diagnosis it was selling the cure for. Turning the ordinary stress of everyday life into a billion tablet a year business and turning millions of patients [music] into long-term dependent customers without ever calling it that. The company's own internal sales training encouraged representatives to frame the drug not as a treatment for a specific illness, but as a generalpurpose solution for the unavoidable friction of modern life. An approach that maximized the size of the potential market almost without limit since nearly everyone at some point experiences stress. By the mid 1970s, the backlash finally arrived and it arrived loudly. Feminist writers and journalists began publicly naming Valium mother's little helper, accusing the medical establishment of sedating women's legitimate anger, grief, and exhaustion instead of ever addressing what was actually causing it. The phrase became the title of a rolling stone song [music] and a genuine cultural flash point. one of the first widespread public challenges to the entire premise that a pill could quietly fix what was underneath it all a social and economic problem. The criticism gained a famous unexpected face [music] in 1978 when former first lady Betty Ford publicly disclosed her own dependence on both alcohol and prescription sedatives. An admission that shocked the country precisely because it [music] came from someone so visible, so respectable, and so far removed from the public's mental image of what an addict was supposed to look like. Her openness helped push the conversation out of whispered gossip columns and into serious national news coverage for the first time. If any of this sounds familiar, a parent, a grandparent, or another relative who always seemed to have a bottle of nerve pills in the cabinet, that quiet detail is more common than most families realize, and it usually traces back to exactly this era. Here is the domino most people never connect and it is the most important one in this entire story. The exact playbook RO used to market Valium downplay the real risk of dependence caught physicians directly with incentives samples and sponsored education and position the drug as the safe solution to a problem. the company itself had helped popularize in the first place becomes the literal template a future pharmaceutical company studies and reuses three decades later when Purdue Pharma launches Oxycontton in the 1990s marketing it to doctors nationwide as a safe lowrisk painkiller with minimal addiction potential. It is running the exact same play the benzoazipene industry ran a full generation earlier. The benzoazipene boom of the 1960s and 70s was not simply a pharmaceutical trend that came and went. It was in a very real sense the dress rehearsal for the opioid crisis that would devastate the country a generation later. The pressure eventually reached the halls of Congress. In 1979, Senator Edward Kennedy chaired formal Senate hearings specifically investigating Valium and the broader pattern of benzoazipene dependence sweeping the country. hearing testimony from patients, physicians, and researchers describing a drug that had been marketed as virtually risk-free and was turning out for a meaningful share of long-term users to be exactly the opposite. It was one of the first times the federal government treated a widely prescribed doctor approved medication with the same scrutiny normally reserved for illegal narcotics. [music] And it marked an early crack in the public confidence that had carried Valium to its billion tablet peak just a year earlier. The story did not stop with Valium either. In 1981, the pharmaceutical company Up John launched Xanax [music] known chemically as alprazolum as a faster acting entry into the same drug class. It worked quickly, which made it popular. But doctors would later realize it was even harder to quit than Valium had ever been. Xanax became the drug that kept showing up case after case in toxicology reports alongside opioids and alcohol in the [music] deaths of major celebrities, transforming what had once been a glamorous persized nerve pill into a recurring headline in overdose autopsies decades later. Investigators studying these overdoses kept finding the same underlying pattern. It was almost never a bzzoazipene acting alone. It was a benzoazipene combined with an opioid [music] painkiller or with alcohol. Each drug quietly suppressing the [music] same basic function, breathing, until the combination overwhelmed a body that might have survived any one of them individually. Another member of the same drug family produced a scandal all its own. Hion, a fast acting sleeping pill sold by Upjon starting in 1982, left a trail of patients reporting something far stranger than ordinary groggginess. Severe memory loss, sudden paranoia, and disturbing personality [music] changes, all after taking nothing more than the dose printed on the bottle. Some patients described losing entire evenings they could not later account for. The stories grew loud enough that Hion was pulled from shelves in the United Kingdom entirely while it kept selling in the United States for years afterward, just with a longer warning label attached. Meaning two patients taking the exact same pill on opposite sides of the Atlantic were quite literally being treated as two different risk levels. Through the 1960s,770s, and 80s, print and television advertising kept reinforcing the same reassuring message year after year. Doctors were shown as trusted, white-coated authority figures, calmly, promising anxious patients that relief was always just one small pill away. These drugs [music] stopped being simply an anxiety treatment somewhere along the way. They became fixtures for insomnia, muscle spasms, seizure disorders, and alcohol withdrawal management. Prescribed routinely across surgery wards, dental offices, and general practice clinics, woven so deeply into the everyday texture of American healthcare that almost nobody thought to question them anymore. By the 2010s, roughly 66 million bzzoazipene prescriptions were being [music] written every single year in the United States alone. That works out to close to one in every three doctor visits for anxiety [music] or sleeprelated complaints, ending with a prescription for a drug from this class. Behind that number were millions of patients quietly renewing the same bottle month after month, year after year because no one, not the pill, not the doctor, not the company that made it, ever told them when or how they were supposed to stop. For decades, the people making these drugs simply did not talk about what happened to patients who stayed on them too long. Company marketing leaned on a single comfortable explanation for anyone who struggled to quit. It was not the drug. It was the anxiety coming back. It is the same trick the [music] tobacco industry ran and the sugar industry after it. Keep the uncomfortable internal findings quiet. let doctors keep prescribing out of habit and let the truth arrive decades later than it should have. When wider guidance limiting long-term use finally showed up in Britain by the late 1980s in the United States, even more slowly and in pieces after that, the pattern of casual refillable, no questions asked prescribing had already had a full generation to take root in ordinary clinics. The exposure when it finally came [music] came slowly and it came almost entirely from the patients themselves. Advocates like Geraldine Burns of Boston who was prescribed Atavan in a hospital after giving birth and left dependent for years afterward began organizing fellow survivors sharing what they had learned the hard way with anyone who would listen. Burns and others like her found that simply being believed was often the hardest part of recovery since many of the physicians they turned to [music] for help had never been taught that a properly prescribed, properly taken medication could produce a withdrawal syndrome this severe and defaulted instead to treating their symptoms as the original anxiety flaring back up rather than a consequence of the treatment itself. In 2022, the documentary film Asscribed brought what advocates now call the benzoazipene crisis into wider public view, following patients who had done nothing wrong by any conventional measure. They took the medication exactly as their doctor instructed, for exactly as long as their doctor recommended, and still ended up with years of disability, unable to work, unable to explain to friends and family why a pill their own physician had prescribed had left them this way. That detail is what makes the story land differently than a typical addiction narrative. [music] Nearly 70% of people who misuse these drugs get [music] them not from a dealer on the street, but from a friend or relative's own medicine cabinet. A fact that reframes the entire crisis as something that grew inside ordinary households rather than outside them. The stakes have not gone away in the present day. Benzoazipines now appear in a significant share of opioid overdose deaths nationwide. [music] The very seditive once marketed as the safe replacement for one dangerous drug class becoming decades later a deadly accelerant when combined with an entirely different one. In 2020, federal regulators finally added a bold amissible warning to every bottle, spelling out in plain language what patients had needed to know for half a century. Taking this pill alongside an opioid can stop your breathing. Public health officials now describe that combination as one of the clearest, most preventable causes of overdose death in the country. A warning that [music] for most of this drug's history simply never reached the people who needed to hear it. This is not simply an American story either. Benzoazipines remain widely prescribed across the entire globe. for anxiety, insomnia, seizure disorders, and alcohol withdrawal. A class of drugs so deeply embedded in modern medicine worldwide [music] that most patients never think to question whether they should be taking it at all. France has historically recorded some of the highest per capita benzoazipene consumption rates in Europe, prompting its own government health warnings and public awareness campaigns aimed at reducing long-term use among older patients. Japan, too, has wrestled with strikingly high long-term prescribing rates, leading regulators there to introduce stricter limits on how many consecutive months a single prescription can cover. Meanwhile, in lower and middle inome countries, access to these drugs is often far less regulated. sold in some regions with minimal prescription oversight at all, meaning the same dependence risks documented in wealthy countries are quietly playing out with even less monitoring and even less support for anyone caught in withdrawal. Long-term users are also disproportionately older adults, a population where these drugs carry their own separate dangers, including a heightened risk of falls, hip fractures, and cognitive decline that can be mistaken for ordinary aging. Studies following older patients [music] through gradual physician supervised tapering have found the process is generally safe even after years of use with most [music] withdrawal symptoms turning out to be mild and short-lived once the reduction is handled carefully and slowly which raises an uncomfortable question. If coming off is manageable with the right support why were so many patients never offered that support in the first place? Today, there is a growing deprescribing movement working to reverse course. Slow physician supervised tapering protocols, [music] dedicated patient support communities, and updated prescribing guidelines are all now trying to undo roughly 50 years of deeply ingrained medical habit. One careful, closely monitored reduction at a time. Online support groups now connect thousands of patients tapering off these drugs simultaneously, trading advice, encouragement, and warnings about withdrawal symptoms that many say their own doctors never mentioned. Effectively building the patient education infrastructure that never existed when the drugs were first prescribed to them. Medical schools have also begun revising how they teach prescribing guidelines for this drug class. With a growing number of newly trained physicians now taught to default toward short-term use and non-drug alternatives first a direct reversal of the casual refillable on day one prescribing culture that defined the 1960s and '7s. A compound a chemist nearly threw into the trash [music] in 1955 went on to outsell every other drug in America within two decades. It was born from a genuine urgent desire to replace a killer. It got accused of quietly sedating [music] a generation of women instead of addressing what was actually wrong. It survived a Senate hearing, a memoir from a former first lady, and a sister drugs ban across the Atlantic. [music] And it still went on to write almost by accident the marketing playbook a future opioid company would study and use to devastating effect. It is still sitting in medicine cabinets across the world right now, waiting in the background of ordinary lives, largely unquestioned, in more homes than almost any other [music] prescription drug in history. If you have ever been prescribed to bzzoazipene, whether for anxiety, for sleep, or for something else entirely, we want to hear your experience. Was it a short prescription [music] that solved the problem and ended cleanly? Or did it turn into something longer and harder to walk away from than you expected?
